===== WORLD 15 · LESSON texture_and_frequency · Texture and frequency =====

TASK w15_1_teach [theory] What supports a frequent c-bet in a given model?
CAPTION: Study texture and frequency.
TEACH: What supports a frequent c-bet in a given model? On A-7-2 rainbow, the ace is high and the other cards are low and far apart. K-3-2 and Q-8-3 rainbow also have one high card and two lower ranks. A three-low flop can still be connected, and middle cards such as 8-7-6 can make several straights. Check which combinations each range brings before betting broadly.
Q: What supports a frequent c-bet in a given model?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] The board favors a broad part of the betting range and opponents respond profitably — Correct. Coverage and responses matter across several hand classes. A dry label alone cannot tell you to bet the whole range.
  - [wrong] Any low-card flop makes a wide c-bet safe — Look again. Low does not mean disconnected. Count the caller’s pairs and straight draws on a connected low board.
    BETTER ANSWER: The board favors a broad part of the betting range and opponents respond profitably
  - [wrong] Having opened before the flop is enough — Look again. The prior raise gives initiative. This flop and the opponent’s continuing range still decide which hands benefit from betting.
    BETTER ANSWER: The board favors a broad part of the betting range and opponents respond profitably

===== WORLD 15 · LESSON protection_and_denial · Protection and denial =====

TASK w15_2_teach [theory] Which result is specifically equity denial?
CAPTION: Study protection and denial.
TEACH: Which result is specifically equity denial? A thin value bet is paid by some worse hands. A bet denies equity when it forces hands with a live chance to improve to fold. A protection bet can do both, but its cost against stronger calls still matters.
Q: Which result is specifically equity denial?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] A live draw folds and cannot use its remaining cards — Correct. Folding ends the draw’s chance to win. That is equity denial even when it never pays your bet.
  - [wrong] A worse pair calls your bet — Look again. That call supplies value. Its equity remains live because it stays in the hand.
    BETTER ANSWER: A live draw folds and cannot use its remaining cards
  - [wrong] A stronger made hand calls at the same size — Look again. The stronger hand still gets to showdown. You also paid into a range that may beat you.
    BETTER ANSWER: A live draw folds and cannot use its remaining cards

  - [wrong] The 9-8 call — Look again. A worse pair paying your bet is a value branch. It stays in and can still improve.
    BETTER ANSWER: The A-K fold
    FEEDBACK TABLE: Flop | You Tc Td | Board 9h 6s 3d | Pot 5.5 BB | Seat BTN | Active btn | Decision btn | Card focus board_0, board_1, board_2 | Facts one pair, overpair, pocket pair, rainbow, backdoor straight
  - [wrong] Both responses remove the opponent’s equity — Look again. Only a fold removes the opponent from the pot. A called hand still has a showdown share.
    BETTER ANSWER: The A-K fold

===== WORLD 15 · LESSON check_back_and_slowplay · Check back and slowplay =====

TASK w15_3_teach [theory] Which fact supports checking back a dry-board set as a trap?
CAPTION: Study check back and slowplay.
TEACH: Which fact supports checking back a dry-board set as a trap? Slowplay means delaying a bet with a very strong hand to keep a later bet possible. On a dry board, weigh the value of that later bet against immediate calls and the free card. If the opponent stays passive or the board gives out many dangerous turns, betting now can earn more.
Q: Which fact supports checking back a dry-board set as a trap?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] The opponent will often bet later with hands that fold now — Correct. A delayed bet can recover value from hands a flop bet drives out. Position lets your check close the current street.
  - [wrong] A set should always disguise its strength — Look again. A passive opponent may check again. Then the free card costs immediate value without adding a later bet.
    BETTER ANSWER: The opponent will often bet later with hands that fold now
  - [wrong] Many draws are eager to pay a bet now — Look again. Those calls favor taking value now. Checking lets the draws see the turn without paying.
    BETTER ANSWER: The opponent will often bet later with hands that fold now

TASK w15_3_read_dry_trap_condition [drill] What makes checking back a candidate here?
CAPTION: BB checks to you. For this read only, suppose BB bluffs many turns after you check back and most of that bluff group folds to a flop bet.
Q: What makes checking back a candidate here?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Flop | You Ac 7c | Board Ad 7h 2s | Pot 5.5 BB | Seat BTN | Active btn | Decision btn | Facts two pair, rainbow
SEATS: UTG folded stack 100 BB | HJ folded stack 100 BB | CO folded stack 100 BB | BTN dealer Ac 7c stack 97.5 BB | SB folded stack 99.5 BB | BB stack 97.5 BB

  + [correct] It keeps the future bluff group in the hand — Correct. A flop bet would fold the stated bluff group. In position, checking closes the flop and keeps those hands available to bet next.
    FEEDBACK TABLE: Flop | You Ac 7c | Board Ad 7h 2s | Pot 5.5 BB | Seat BTN | Active btn | Decision btn | Card focus board_0, board_1, board_2 | Facts two pair, rainbow
  - [wrong] The top two pair can no longer be overtaken — Look again. The turn and river can still change the winner. The trap depends on the later bets being worth that risk.
    BETTER ANSWER: It keeps the future bluff group in the hand
    FEEDBACK TABLE: Flop | You Ac 7c | Board Ad 7h 2s | Pot 5.5 BB | Seat BTN | Active btn | Decision btn | Card focus board_0, board_1, board_2 | Facts two pair, rainbow
  - [wrong] BB has already promised to call a big turn bet — Look again. The premise gives a future lead policy for BB. It says nothing about paying a large bet from you.
    BETTER ANSWER: It keeps the future bluff group in the hand
    FEEDBACK TABLE: Flop | You Ac 7c | Board Ad 7h 2s | Pot 5.5 BB | Seat BTN | Active btn | Decision btn | Card focus board_0, board_1, board_2 | Facts two pair, rainbow

===== WORLD 15 · LESSON monotone_and_paired · Monotone and paired =====

TASK w15_4_teach [theory] What should change your bet plan on these textures?
CAPTION: Study monotone and paired.
TEACH: What should change your bet plan on these textures? A monotone flop has three cards of one suit. A paired flop repeats a rank. On a monotone flop, count two-card holdings that already make a flush. On a paired flop, count trips, full houses and quads separately from ordinary pairs.
Q: What should change your bet plan on these textures?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts

  - [wrong] Whether the paired rank is high, by itself — Look again. A high pair gives clues about which opens contain trips. The caller can still hold trips or a full house. Count both ranges.
    BETTER ANSWER: Which strong combinations survive in each range
  - [wrong] The preflop raiser never has good flush coverage — Look again. Suit-blocked classes determine the legal flushes. The label preflop raiser does not supply those counts.
    BETTER ANSWER: Which strong combinations survive in each range

===== WORLD 15 · LESSON leads_and_stabs · Leads and stabs =====

TASK w15_5_teach [theory] What distinguishes a lead from a stab in this course?
CAPTION: Study leads and stabs.
TEACH: What distinguishes a lead from a stab in this course? An out-of-position bet before the preflop aggressor acts is a lead, sometimes called a donk bet. A stab is a bet after the aggressor shows weakness by checking. The same board can offer both ideas in different action orders.
Q: What distinguishes a lead from a stab in this course?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] Whether you bet before the aggressor acts or after their check — Correct. Read who raised preflop and who has already acted on the flop. That separates a lead from a stab.
  - [wrong] Whether the bet is larger than the pot — Look again. Amount is a sizing choice. The names here describe positions and action order.
    BETTER ANSWER: Whether you bet before the aggressor acts or after their check
  - [wrong] Whether you have two pair or a bluff — Look again. Hand strength can affect why you bet. It does not change which action came before the bet.
    BETTER ANSWER: Whether you bet before the aggressor acts or after their check

===== WORLD 15 · LESSON check_raise_and_checkpoint · Check raise and checkpoint =====

TASK w15_6_teach [theory] What makes a flop raising range merged?
CAPTION: Study check raise and checkpoint.
TEACH: What makes a flop raising range merged? A check-raise follows your check and the opponent’s bet. A polarized raise range emphasizes very strong hands and bluffs with equity. A merged raise can include hands between those ends, such as strong top pair, when worse hands call. Texture and the response decide which approach fits.
Q: What makes a flop raising range merged?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] Some strong one-pair hands raise alongside stronger hands — Correct. That middle value band connects the raise range between its strongest hands and weaker candidates. The calls must justify including it.
  - [wrong] Only sets and high-equity semibluffs raise — Look again. That describes a polarized shape. Strong one-pair hands stay in the calling range in that policy.
    BETTER ANSWER: Some strong one-pair hands raise alongside stronger hands
  - [wrong] Every raise uses the same amount — Look again. One amount can serve either a merged or polarized range. Identify which hands use it.
    BETTER ANSWER: Some strong one-pair hands raise alongside stronger hands

TASK w15_6_read_polar_on_two_tone [drill] Which policy is polarized for a check-raise here?
CAPTION: No BB hole cards are revealed. Think of these as candidate holdings in a policy. The modeled top-pair hands call rather than raise.
Q: Which policy is polarized for a check-raise here?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Flop | Board Qh 7c 2h | Pot 7.5 BB | To call 2 BB | Seat BB | Active bb | Decision bb | Facts two-tone
EFFECTIVE: BTN 97.5
SEATS: UTG folded stack 100 BB | HJ folded stack 100 BB | CO folded stack 100 BB | BTN dealer stack 95.5 BB bet 2 BB | SB folded stack 99.5 BB | BB stack 97.5 BB
TRAIL: preflop: SB posts 0.5 BB · preflop: BB posts 1 BB · preflop: UTG folds · preflop: HJ folds · preflop: CO folds · preflop: BTN raises to 2.5 BB · preflop: SB folds · preflop: BB calls 1.5 BB · flop: BB checks · flop: BTN bets 2 BB
  + [correct] Raise sets and the Ah Jh or Kh Jh flush draws — Correct. Sets form the strong end. The two named draws are the semibluff end, and the modeled top pairs are left in calls.
  - [wrong] Raise sets and strong top pairs together — Look again. Including top pair alongside sets is a more merged value shape. That is a different policy from the one described.
    BETTER ANSWER: Raise sets and the Ah Jh or Kh Jh flush draws
  - [wrong] Raise only top pair because the board has two hearts — Look again. Top pair alone spans neither end of a polarized range. The suit texture does not make that policy polarized.
    BETTER ANSWER: Raise sets and the Ah Jh or Kh Jh flush draws

===== WORLD 16 · LESSON commitment_and_defense · Commitment and defense =====

TASK w16_2_teach [theory] Which inputs determine the break-even equity for one terminal call?
CAPTION: Minimum defense frequency addresses how often a whole range continues against a zero-equity bluff. A hand’s break-even equity answers whether this one call pays at its price.
TEACH: Which inputs determine the break-even equity for one terminal call? Minimum defense frequency addresses how often a whole range continues against a zero-equity bluff. A hand’s break-even equity answers whether this one call pays at its price.
Q: Which inputs determine the break-even equity for one terminal call?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] The call amount and the final pot — Correct. A hand breaks even when equity times the final pot repays its new call cost.
  - [wrong] The old chips you personally added — Look again. The old chips belong to the pot. The new call has to justify its own cost.
    BETTER ANSWER: The call amount and the final pot
  - [wrong] The range’s minimum defense frequency alone — Look again. That frequency counts defended combinations. It does not tell this hand how much of a showdown pot it wins.
    BETTER ANSWER: The call amount and the final pot

===== WORLD 16 · LESSON streets_of_value · Streets of value =====

TASK w16_3_teach [theory] What makes a one-street value plan sensible?
CAPTION: Plan value by street. On each street ask which worse hands still call after the previous action and how the runout changed them.
TEACH: What makes a one-street value plan sensible? Plan value by street. On each street ask which worse hands still call after the previous action and how the runout changed them.
Q: What makes a one-street value plan sensible?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] The worse hands pay once, then the later call range becomes too strong — Correct. Collect where worse hands still pay. Reassess rather than locking in all later bets.
  - [wrong] A top pair must bet exactly twice — Look again. The hand label cannot tell you which weaker combinations survive the first bet.
    BETTER ANSWER: The worse hands pay once, then the later call range becomes too strong
  - [wrong] A strong flop guarantees three streets — Look again. Turn and river cards can improve the caller or remove worse calls. Check the remaining range on each street.

  - [wrong] The caller leads after the raiser checks the flop — Look again. That is a probe by the preflop caller.

===== WORLD 16 · LESSON pressure_and_blocking · Pressure and blocking =====

TASK w16_5_teach [theory] When can a block bet lower your showdown cost?
CAPTION: A turn overbet compresses the calling range and changes the river stack-to-pot ratio. A small river block bet can set a price only if the opponent usually accepts that price.
TEACH: When can a block bet lower your showdown cost? A turn overbet compresses the calling range and changes the river stack-to-pot ratio. A small river block bet can set a price only if the opponent usually accepts that price.
Q: When can a block bet lower your showdown cost?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] When the opponent calls many worse hands and rarely raises that size — Correct. Compare this branch with what the opponent bets if you check. A small lead cannot stop an opponent who will raise.
  - [wrong] Every time you act first — Look again. Position only supplies the option to bet. Opponent responses determine the cost.
    BETTER ANSWER: When the opponent calls many worse hands and rarely raises that size
  - [wrong] Whenever you want to deny a river draw — Look again. The final board is complete on the river. This bet is about response and showdown cost.
    BETTER ANSWER: When the opponent calls many worse hands and rarely raises that size
